title: Samson's last prayer (Judges 16:23–30)
hook: blind and shackled, the strong man prays one more time

segments.voice: Yesterday, three hundred: the army made smaller. Your line was less is enough.

"Call for Samson, that he may make us sport." The lords of the Philistines have gathered at the temple of their god Dagon, and they say their god has delivered their enemy into their hand. The enemy is Samson, Israel's strong man: betrayed by Delilah, his hair shaved, his eyes put out, bound with fetters of brass and set to grinding in the prison house. A boy leads him out by the hand. The text says about three thousand men and women watch from the roof alone. And there's one small line, a few verses back, that the reader knows and the crowd doesn't.
screen: `A BOY LEADS HIM BY THE HAND.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-two: "Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven." Samson asks the boy to let him feel the pillars the house stands on. Then he prays, in the King James Bible: "O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes." This isn't a gentle prayer. Samson asks for revenge. Some readers sum up his whole story that way: strong, impulsive, careless with the vow over his life. Yet the text keeps this prayer, and it's answered. Look at the first words, before the anger: remember me. And only this once. He seems to know he has no credit left. Then: "Let me die with the Philistines." He bows himself with all his might, the pillars give way, and the house falls on the lords and the people. The chapter closes with a grim tally: those he killed at his death were more than those he killed in his life. Readers don't agree on how to hear this ending. Some hear a sacrifice. Some hear a tragedy, a man whose strength was never matched by wisdom. Hebrews eleven reaches him in a hurry. The writer runs out of room and lists names: "the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson." No verdict, just the name, beside the man from the winepress. Some readers say that's enough: blind, shackled and mocked, he still knew whom to call.

Let your attention go to a place where you're not strong right now: something you've lost, a mistake you keep paying for, a part of life that feels shackled, and don't dress it up; Samson didn't. If you pray, borrow only the first words of his prayer, remember me, and then stop. If you don't pray, hold that weak place gently, the way you'd hold someone else's.
Dagon. The Philistine god whose temple the lords filled to mock blind, shackled Samson, and whose house came down when Samson pushed the pillars.
Your line: remember me, just this once. Two plain words came first. That's day seven hundred six.

howItsDone: Christians read Samson's story in more than one way, as a warning about strength without wisdom and as a sign that a prayer from the lowest place is still heard, and some point out that Hebrews 11:32 still lists his name.

chat.says: Samson's last prayer sounds angry. Why do people still find something in it?
options: Before the anger, he asks God to remember him, and the prayer is answered.
Because he forgives the Philistines at the end, the way a saint would.
Because the prayer asks for nothing at all, only to praise God's name.
chat.meaning: His prayer asks for revenge, but it opens with remember me, only this once. The text keeps it, and the prayer is answered.

notes: 'About three thousand men and women' on the roof is from Judges 16:27.
'Careless with the vow over his life' and 'careless with what he was given' summarize the earlier Samson chapters (13:5 Nazirite vow; 14–16); interpretive. Confirm the tone is fair.
The prayer for vengeance is presented honestly, with two readings of the ending (sacrifice; tragedy) offered without ranking. The closing 'he still knew whom to call' is attributed to 'some readers'.
The practice offers only the real words 'remember me' from Judges 16:28 for those who pray; no new prayer is written.
